trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, this trail typically stays snow-covered into early summer and doesn't fully open until around July; stay on the boardwalk at all times since the ground around the fumaroles and mudpots can be thin-crusted and scalding underneath.
trails.didYouKnow: Bumpass Hell is named for a 19th-century guide who fell through the crust and severely burned his leg, later using the story to draw paying tourists to the site.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the Lassen Peak Trail is snow-covered outside of roughly July through October and NPS posts current conditions at go.nps.gov/lavo/hike — check that page before you go, since exact opening dates shift year to year with snowpack.
trails.didYouKnow: Lassen Peak is one of the largest plug dome volcanoes in the world and last erupted in a series of explosions between 1914 and 1917.

trails.trailTip: The lower loop past the falls includes a rock staircase section that can be slick when wet, so take the gentler Cascades return route if footing looks unstable.
trails.didYouKnow: Kings Creek Falls drops about 30 feet over a basalt cliff formed by lava flows from the volcanic activity that shaped the park.

trails.trailTip: Popular at sunrise for reflection photos of Lassen Peak across the water; the trail is mostly flat and shaded, making it a good option even on a smoke-hazy day.
trails.didYouKnow: Manzanita Lake was formed roughly 300 years ago when a rockfall/mudflow off Chaos Crags dammed the creek that fills it.

trails.trailTip: The final climb is through loose volcanic cinder that slides underfoot, so expect a slower pace than the mileage suggests and bring extra water since there's no shade near the summit.
trails.didYouKnow: The Cinder Cone's summit crater is ringed by the colorful Painted Dunes, oxidized volcanic ash deposited by an eruption in the 1650s.

trails.trailTip: The upper mile is exposed switchbacks along a ridge with little shade or water, so start early to avoid afternoon thunderstorms common at this elevation in summer.
trails.didYouKnow: Brokeoff Mountain is a remnant of ancient Mount Tehama, a massive stratovolcano that collapsed roughly 350,000 years ago, of which Lassen Peak is a much younger offshoot.

trails.trailTip: Stay on the paved walkway and behind railings near the mudpots — the ground beyond the barriers can be unstable and the steam vents release sulfur gas that's unhealthy to breathe up close.
trails.didYouKnow: Sulphur Works sits near the center of the collapsed ancient Mount Tehama caldera, making it one of the most accessible thermal areas in the park.

trails.trailTip: Peak wildflower bloom in the meadow is typically mid-to-late summer; trail can be muddy early season from snowmelt, so waterproof footwear helps.
trails.didYouKnow: Paradise Meadow floods seasonally with meltwater, creating the shallow lily pond that gives this trail its informal name.

animals.whereToLook: Forests and meadows throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: If you see a bear, watch from your car or from at least 100 yards with binoculars and never leave food accessible to draw one closer for a photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Lassen's black bears den up for winter dormancy that can last from November into April at this elevation.

animals.whereToLook: Mixed conifer forest edges and meadows
animals.viewingTip: Deer here are used to roadside viewing, but keep a respectful distance and never offer food, which habituates them to humans and vehicles.
animals.didYouKnow: Mule deer are named for their oversized, mule-like ears, which give them excellent hearing to detect predators.

animals.viewingTip: Enjoy their calls at dusk from a distance; never approach or feed a coyote, as habituated coyotes become a safety problem for both people and the animal.
animals.didYouKnow: Coyote howls and yips heard at dusk are often a family group communicating territory boundaries to neighboring packs.

animals.whereToLook: Near the Lassen Peak and Bumpass Hell trailheads
animals.viewingTip: These birds are famously bold around people, but resist the urge to hand-feed them — human food harms their health and encourages aggressive begging.
animals.didYouKnow: A single Clark's Nutcracker can cache tens of thousands of pine seeds each fall and rely on spatial memory to relocate them months later.

animals.whereToLook: Volcanic talus slopes near Bumpass Hell and Lassen Peak
animals.viewingTip: Sit quietly near a talus field and listen for their sharp call; watch with binoculars rather than climbing into the rockpile, which can crush their den spaces.
animals.didYouKnow: Pikas are extremely sensitive to heat and can die from prolonged exposure above about 78°F, making them a bellwether species for a warming climate.

animals.whereToLook: Meadows and forest edges, especially west side of the park
animals.viewingTip: View from a distance with binoculars; during fall rut, give bucks extra space since they can be unpredictable when competing for mates.
animals.didYouKnow: Black-tailed deer are a coastal subspecies of mule deer, generally smaller with a darker, fully black-topped tail.

animals.viewingTip: Often mistaken for a chipmunk; enjoy watching them forage naturally and never feed them, since human food causes serious digestive harm to small rodents.
animals.didYouKnow: Unlike chipmunks, golden-mantled ground squirrels lack facial stripes — only the stripes on their sides continue the resemblance.

animals.whereToLook: Volcanic cliff faces near Brokeoff Mountain and Sulphur Works
animals.viewingTip: Watch nesting cliffs from a distance with binoculars or a spotting scope and respect any posted seasonal closures around active eyries during nesting season.
animals.didYouKnow: Peregrine falcons can reach speeds over 200 mph in a hunting stoop, making them the fastest animal on Earth.
